extracted.intended_audience: small businesses and small-entity representatives preparing public comments on proposed federal regulations
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for small businesses to prepare effective public comment letters to federal agencies on proposed rules, including structure, argumentation, evidence, tone, and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the Rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the Federal Register notice and identify the highest-impact areas of the proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully read the agency's notice to find which provisions will most affect your business; focus comments on those high-impact areas so the agency can easily see relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be Clear and Concise
rubrics_metrics.description: State purpose early; use plain language and avoid jargon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead with your main point or purpose in the introduction and at the start of each section. Keep sentences and paragraphs short, use plain English, and avoid technical jargon that obscures your point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain Business Impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide concrete examples, cost estimates, and data describing how the rule would affect your business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify impacts where possible (e.g., compliance costs, staffing, equipment, paperwork, revenue impacts). Tie specific provisions to concrete business effects so agencies can assess real-world consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer Solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggest practical alternatives or modifications and explain their benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propose workable regulatory changes (e.g., alternative language, deadlines extensions, industry-specific exclusions) and explain how each alternative mitigates harms while meeting regulatory objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain Professionalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a respectful, constructive tone and follow agency submission instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid anger, sarcasm, or ad hominem language. Follow formatting and submission rules in the notice so your comment is accepted and considered. Professional tone increases credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment Letter Structure — Introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify who you are, the rule name, your business background, and provide a summary of concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with a concise statement of identity and interest (e.g., size/type of business), cite the specific rule or docket, and summarize the key points you will raise so reviewers immediately understand your perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment Letter Structure — Body
rubrics_metrics.description: Lay out which provisions you support or oppose with explanations and supporting data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize the body by issue or regulatory section. For each point, state your claim, provide evidence (data, examples), and connect the evidence to the claimed impact. When using data, avoid disclosing confidential information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment Letter Structure — Conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a brief summary and thank the agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Close with a short restatement of your main request or recommendation and a courteous closing; this reinforces the action you want the agency to take.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-Component Argument Framework — Claim
rubrics_metrics.description: State your main argument at the beginning of each section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin each section with a clear claim so reviewers immediately see the point before presenting supporting evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-Component Argument Framework — Supporting Data
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantify impacts using data such as agency cost assumptions, compliance expenses, and revenue effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide numbers, cost estimates, and concrete examples; cite sources and document where data came from so the agency can verify and rely on your evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-Component Argument Framework — Impact Statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Connect evidence to the claim and recommend specific remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how the presented data supports your claim and then propose targeted remedies (e.g., specific regulatory text changes, timeline adjustments, exclusions) that address the identified harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be Specific and Document Sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide the most specific information possible and cite sources for data and assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "The more specific information you can provide, the better." Include citations and documentation of data origins to establish reliability and allow agency reviewers to verify facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish Credibility with Relevant Experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate relevant field experience to bolster the weight of your comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Briefly describe your business's qualifications, experience, or market role that make your perspective informed and reliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect Confidential Information
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide data without disclosing confidential business information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting data, avoid revealing proprietary or confidential details; consider using aggregated or redacted figures and follow any agency guidance on confidential submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing — Submit Early
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment periods typically span 30–60 days; submit early to allow agency consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File comments well before the deadline to increase the chance they will be reviewed and considered during agency decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofread and Peer Review
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofread your comment and have someone else review it or read it aloud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminate typos, unclear phrasing, and logical gaps. A second pair of eyes can catch issues you miss and improve clarity and persuasiveness.
